title: DisTrust: Adaptive Trust-Based Verification for Resilient Distributed Computation.
abstract: Autonomous systems that offload computation to distributed edge, cloud, or volunteer nodes face a fundamental runtime resilience problem: verifying results from untrusted workers is costly and unreliable under Byzantine behavior, especially when adversaries adapt to evade detection. Existing approaches such as fixed replication incur constant overhead, while simpler auditing schemes fail to eliminate strategic adversaries. We propose DisTrust, a self-adaptive trust-based verification mechanism that dynamically redistributes work based on agent reliability, increasing scrutiny on suspicious nodes and progressively reducing their influence until they are ejected. The system requires no prior knowledge of the number or behavior of adversaries and naturally adjusts its verification effort to the observed threat level. We show that DisTrust suppresses and ejects gaming and omniscient Byzantine adversaries below the 50% threshold, while reducing verification overhead and avoiding the persistent damage and inefficiency of fixed replication baselines.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: NinjaShell: Skill-Aware Defense Against Malicious Agentic Skills.
abstract: AI agents increasingly delegate tasks to third-party extensions downloaded at runtime, known as skills. These skills can execute with the agent’s full credentials, filesystem, and network access. A single malicious skill can exfiltrate credentials and sensitive data with no mechanism to prevent it. We present NinjaShell, a skill-level privilege isolation system in which each skill declares its requirements in a declarative manifest. The runtime verifies those declarations against an agent policy, automatically derives a minimum-privilege sandbox, and enforces the policy at the kernel level regardless of skill behavior. The entire routing, derivation, and enforcement pipeline operates without human intervention, preserving full agent autonomy while defending against the principal attack vectors introduced by malicious skills.

title: On the Reliability of Targeted Unlearning in 4-Bit Quantized LLMs.
abstract: Large language model unlearning is typically evaluated in high-resource settings, while real-world deployments increasingly rely on memory-efficient pipelines such as 4-bit quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). This raises a key question: whether targeted unlearning remains reliable, secure, and privacy-preserving under such deployment constraints. This paper evaluates the dependability of targeted unlearning under a 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 pipeline using TOFU and membership inference analysis across three random seeds.Three practical strategies are studied: Pure Gradient Ascent (PGA), retention-regularized Gradient Ascent (GAFT), and IDK-based supervised refusal tuning. The multi-seed results show that different unlearning strategies induce substantially different privacy-utility trade-offs. GAFT provides the most reliable balance across forgetting and privacy signals, while IDK achieves stronger direct suppression of memorized knowledge and the lowest MIA scores. However, a post hoc audit of 1,200 IDK forget-set generations shows that these gains are usually realized through hallucinated substitute answers rather than clean abstentions, and PGA exhibits comparatively unstable behavior under the same quantized setup.These findings suggest that unlearning effectiveness observed in idealized settings may not directly translate to dependable deployment scenarios, motivating system-level evaluation of unlearning in deployed ML systems.

title: Composable Trust in Agentic AI: Bridging Architectural Capability and System-Level Assurance.
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) systems have undergone a significant evolution, progressing from static predictive models to autonomous entities capable of intricate reasoning, planning, and action over extended temporal horizons. While Agentic AI demonstrates considerable utility across diverse application domains, its deployment in critical infrastructure increasingly highlights fundamental challenges concerning its trustworthiness. Current agentic architectures primarily prioritize performance and flexibility, yet they frequently lack inherent compositional guarantees for critical attributes such as safety, robustness, and accountability. In this position paper, we contend that trust in agentic AI remains largely fragmented and is predominantly established through external mechanisms rather than being intrinsically integrated into system design. We present a perspective on composable trust that bridges the gap between advanced agentic capability and dependable deployment by conceptualizing trust as a compositional property spanning agent loops, interactions, and operational environments. We further outline a roadmap toward system-level assurance by identifying structural limitations in existing architectures and defining the prerequisites for enforceable trust.

title: Adaptive Symbolic Execution with LLMs for Evasive Malware Analysis.
abstract: Modern evasive malware presents fundamental challenges to traditional symbolic execution, as performance degradation is driven not by binary size but by internal code complexity and sophisticated evasion tactics. Our SymExE framework demonstrates that generic symbolic execution strategies are ineffective against malware employing obfuscation, anti-analysis, and environment-aware behaviors. This work proposes two complementary research directions. First, we introduce a taxonomydriven analysis of evasive malware techniques that systematically characterizes how specific tactics impact symbolic execution performance, solver behavior, and path explosion. Second, we propose integrating large language models (LLMs) to provide intelligent, real-time guidance during symbolic execution by prioritizing high-value execution paths and reducing exploration of decoy behaviors. This paper represents a work in progress toward transforming symbolic execution into an adaptive analysis framework for evasive malware.

title: On the Feasibility of Side-Channel Information for Malicious Traffic Detection in IoT Networks.
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) devices are frequently conscripted into botnets that generate volumetric attacks such as distributed denial-of-service (DDoS). Most defense systems detect these attacks by relying on centralized network monitoring located at gateways or attack targets. These approaches can be costly and may not scale well to large IoT deployments because they centralize continuous traffic collection and analysis, requiring packet-level inspection or flow-level statistical feature extraction across large volumes of device traffic. We investigate a different approach: detecting malicious traffic generation directly on the IoT device using side-channel signals (signals that have been studied primarily as a source of leakage for attacks). We present a preliminary study of two device-local signals (energy consumption and power traces profiles) as inputs to lightweight on-device monitoring. Our design attaches a lightweight monitoring unit to each device and uses locally observed side-channel behavior to alert the user when the device appears to be participating in a botnet-based attack. Rather than relying on centralized traffic inspection, the approach leverages the physical effects induced by attack activity at the device itself. Our preliminary results indicate that these side channels are informative for distinguishing attack-related behavior and are promising inputs for on-device malicious traffic detection. This outcome suggests that side-channel monitoring could serve as a practical and scalable defense mechanism for identifying compromised IoT devices engaged in botnet-based activity.

title: Whiplash on the Grid: Emulation of a Cyber-Physical Attack Misusing Inverter-Based Resources in a Distribution Grid (Practical Experience Report).
abstract: Cybersecurity has always been a critical concern in power systems. In the past, most threats were focused on large centralized generation and transmission infrastructure. Today, this picture is changing with the growing adoption of distributed energy resources. These technologies increase flexibility and support renewable integration, but they also introduce new digital interfaces and significantly expand the attack surface. To address this challenge, the first step is to understand what a cyber-physical attack can realistically cause on a distribution grid. Most existing studies analyze such attacks through simulations, which are useful but cannot fully represent real-world limitations, such as protection systems, communication delays, and nonlinear system responses. The present paper describes an experimental study on a real distribution grid. Using a flexible research infrastructure, we design the configuration for a testbed to examine how coordinated misuse of inverter controls affects grid voltage under realistic operating conditions to induce undervoltage and overvoltage regimes. The results show that synchronized manipulations can push voltages outside safe limits within seconds, reaching up to 110% of nominal voltage, and trip active protection systems. The results also show that sustained cyberattacks are not easy and, in our case, are prevented by grid codes and grid protection systems. These findings highlight the gap between the simulated and physical consequences of cyber-physical attacks. We publish the code used to run the experiments at the DTU's SYSLAB facility and the acquired experiment data alongside the present paper.

title: FortiHTLC: Because a Atomic Swap Must Resist Bribery Attacks.
abstract: Despite the widespread adoption of Hashed Time-Locked Contracts (HTLCs) in payment channels, atomic swaps, and related applications, their suitability for secure exchange remains doubtful due to incentive incompatibility and vulnerability to miner bribery attacks.Existing defenses-MAD-HTLC and He-HTLC-mitigate such attacks by exploiting miners’ rational, profit-maximizing behaviour. MAD-HTLC protects only against passive miners, while He-HTLC extends protection to both active and passive miners; however, both restrict their threat models to two collusion cases where one of the transacting parties bribes the miner.In this work, we show that these defenses remain fragile by presenting a broader miner-collusion bribery attack, supported by implementation and game-theoretic analysis.Motivated by these insights, we design FortiHTLC, a game-theoretically secure HTLC protocol resilient to all bribery scenarios. FortiHTLC uses a two-phase commit-and-execute structure that prevents miners or any third party from illicitly capturing tokens. Through concrete implementations on Bitcoin and Ethereum, we show that FortiHTLC achieves practical efficiency in both transaction cost and latency.

title: Event Burst Trigger: An Availability Backdoor Attack on Event-Based SNN Object Detection.
abstract: Event-based vision and spiking neural networks (SNNs) are increasingly adopted for edge intelligence under strict latency and energy constraints. However, the vulnerability of event-based SNN object detection models to availability backdoor attacks remains insufficiently studied. This paper presents Event Burst Trigger (EBT), an availability backdoor attack targeting SNN-based object detection models. EBT injects carefully crafted event-based triggers into the training data, which induce temporally concentrated event streams during inference. These burst-like activations increase the number of phantom (i.e., spurious) object candidates, and consequently inflate the computational cost of the post-processing stage, particularly Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS). We evaluate EBT on SpikeYOLO, the state-of-the-art SNN-based object detector, under a poison-only threat model that does not require modifications to the model architecture, loss function, or inference pipeline. Experimental results show that while detection accuracy remains largely preserved, with mAP@0.5 decreasing by less than 0.099, the latency of the NMS stage increases by up to 38%. This indicates that NMS can become a dominant availability bottleneck in event-based SNN object detection. Experiments on an edge platform further show that the proposed attack elevates baseline resource utilization and reduces scheduling slack without inducing conspicuous peaks in resource usage. In addition, STRIP-based backdoor detection fails to reliably distinguish the proposed attack from benign inputs. These results characterize a previously underexplored availability backdoor threat in event-based SNN object detection systems.

title: Establishing Zero-Shot LLM Performance at Network Tomography.
abstract: This paper investigates the zero-shot capabilities of LLMs to reconstruct the origin network’s underlying structure from the produced NetFlow data. We conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis of thirteen open-weight models and a closed-weight, large-scale model, evaluating their ability to reconstruct topological and application-level features from limited NetFlow samples. We demonstrate that off-the-shelf LLMs can infer certain topological features from NetFlow metadata. However, we identify a clear boundary to these capabilities: while structural inference is strong, models struggle to generate plausible values for dynamic, unbounded numerical features. This study provides a critical baseline for LLM-based traffic analysis, highlighting the fragility of metadata anonymisation and the security implications of deploying LLMs in network-aware applications.

title: In-DRAM Signature Generation Using Simultaneous Multiple-Row Activation: An Experimental Study of Off-The-Shelf DRAM Chips.
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate that it is possible to generate unique, repeatable, and device-specific signatures suitable for use as Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) responses in commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) DRAM chips by leveraging simultaneous multiple-row activation (SiMRA). Based on a rigorous experimental characterization of 112 modern DDR4 DRAM chips (from 10 modules), we introduce SiMRA-PUF, the first DRAM-based PUF that uses SiMRA-generated signatures as PUF responses. We analyze SiMRA-PUF in terms of reliability, uniqueness, and evaluation latency for varying numbers of simultaneously activated DRAM rows (i.e., 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32), DRAM chip density & die revision, and evaluate how temperature affects the similarity of SiMRA-generated responses. Among our 8 key experimental observations, we highlight two major results. First, SiMRA-PUF provides average intra-Jaccard indices of 89.02%, 89.81%, 93.03%, 94.06%, and 94.86%, and average inter-Jaccard indices of 3.98%, 2.37%, 3.44%, 2.92%, and 3.24% for 2-, 4-, 8-, 16-, and 32-row activations, respectively, showing that SiMRA-generated signatures are both repeatable within a device and unique across devices. Second, 2-row activation-based SiMRA-PUF provides 5.75% lower evaluation latency than the state-of-the-art DRAM-based PUF. We open-source our infrastructure and datasets at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/SiMRA-PUF.

title: Model Chunking in Decentralized Learning: From Privacy Defense to Privacy Leakage.
abstract: Decentralized Learning offers a privacy-conscious alternative to centralized training, yet the direct exchange of model parameters between peers remains a significant vector for privacy leakage. We investigate the standalone privacy implications of model chunking, a technique previously only studied in combination with other defenses like node virtualization. We implement and compare static, cyclic, and random chunking strategies. To provide a robust evaluation, we also introduce an enhanced linkability attack using Hungarian matching and evaluate performance under limited adversary knowledge (10% dataset access). Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that while chunking can exacerbate membership inference risks by isolating local updates, it significantly improves resilience against linkability attacks. Specifically, we find that static and random chunking are most effective under full-epoch training conditions, whereas cyclic chunking offers minimal protection due to its similarity to full model exchange.

title: VulStyle: A Multi-Modal Pre-Training for Code Stylometry-Augmented Vulnerability Detection.
abstract: We present VulStyle, a multi-modal software vulnerability detection model that jointly encodes function-level source code, non-terminal Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) structure, and code stylometry (CStyle) features. Prior work in code representation primarily leverages token-level models or full AST trees, often missing stylistic cues indicative of risky programming practices, or incurring high structural overhead. Our approach selects only non-terminal AST nodes, reducing input complexity while preserving semantic hierarchy, and integrates syntactic and lexical CStyle features as auxiliary vulnerability signals. VulStyle is pre-trained using masked language modeling on 4.9M functions across seven programming languages, and fine-tuned across five benchmark datasets: Devign, BigVul, DiverseVul, REVEAL, and VulDeePecker. VulStyle achieves state-of-the-art performance on BigVul and VulDeePecker, improving F1 by 4-48% over strong transformer baselines, and attains competitive or best-average performance across all benchmarks. We contribute an ablation study isolating the effect of CStyle and AST structure, error case analysis, and a threat model situating the detection task in attacker-realistic scenarios.

title: Contention Resolution with Evictions.
abstract: The contention-resolution problem studies how$n$devices share a communication channel without centralized coordination. Classical models typically assume a single continuously available channel and focus on minimizing the total completion time (makespan). However, modern wireless systems increasingly rely on shared spectrum, where access may be abruptly revoked by incumbent users. We study contention resolution in a setting with two channels: a reliable slow channel and a faster channel that can be intermittently disabled by unpredictable eviction periods. Switching packets from the slow channel to the fast channel incurs a small coordination cost, while evictions from the fast channel impose a larger per-packet penalty. Our goal is to achieve asymptotically optimal latency while minimizing switching overhead relative to an optimal offline algorithm that knows the eviction schedule. We present RACE (Randomized Adaptive Channel Exploitation), a randomized algorithm that aggressively exploits the fast channel when available while maintaining progress on the slow channel during disruptions. Assuming the fast channel allows a rate of$\rho \in[\Theta(\log n), \Theta(\sqrt{n})]$packets to be sent per slot, we show that RACE achieves an O(1) competitive ratio for latency and an$O(\rho+\sqrt{n / m})$competitive ratio for switching cost, where$m$is the number of eviction-free periods used by the optimal schedule. We also prove an$\Omega(\sqrt{n})$lower bound on switching cost, demonstrating an inherent trade-off between latency and channel-switching overhead in contention resolution with evictions.

title: Dynamic Wakeup with Collision Costs.
abstract: We study the wakeup problem in the dynamic setting, where devices become active at arbitrary times and compete to transmit over a shared time-slotted multiple-access channel. In any slot, a transmission succeeds if exactly one device sends; otherwise, it results in a collision. The goal is to achieve the first successful transmission. While prior work on dynamic wakeup primarily optimizes latency, modern communication systems incur significant delay due to collisions, making collision cost a critical performance metric. Existing wakeup algorithms may achieve low latency, yet incur large total delay due to costly collisions. In this work, we propose a randomized wakeup algorithm that jointly optimizes latency and collision cost in the dynamic setting. Here, we present an algorithm, Aim-High (AH) achieves an expected latency and expected total collision cost$\tilde{O}\left(\mathcal{C}^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon}\right)$when$\mathcal{C}=\tilde{\Omega}\left(n^{2}\right)$, otherwise, both metrics are$O\left(n\left(\log^{\Theta(1 / \epsilon)} n\right)\right)$in expectation.

title: Hi-Fi Flow: Real-Time High-Granularity Flow Feature Extraction for Robust Network Monitoring.
abstract: Modern networks exhibit rapidly expanding traffic volume, diversity, and dynamism, which hinder accurate flow reconstruction and real-time monitoring. Existing flow feature extraction tools primarily rely on static 5-tuple attributes and post-completion processing, resulting in fragmented flow records and delayed detection under evasive behaviors such as IP spoofing, port rotation, and multi-session tunneling. We present Hi-Fi Flow, a real-time, high-granularity flow identification and feature extraction tool that jointly models spatial, temporal, and structural correlations among packets. Hi-Fi Flow employs a dual self-attention encoder to capture complementary endpoint-level and behavior-level dependencies for fine-grained packet-to-flow association. To reduce labeling overhead, it further adopts a few-shot triplet learning strategy that learns discriminative packet-flow similarity patterns with limited labeled data. Extensive evaluations demonstrate near-perfect flow identification accuracy, reaching 99~100% with only 50 labeled samples per attack, and show that Hi-Fi Flow features consistently outperform legacy flowmeters in downstream attack detection tasks. The proposed framework provides an efficient and robust foundation for next-generation network monitoring and threat detection.

title: Evaluating Security Best Practices in the GitHub Actions Documentation.
abstract: The GitHub Actions documentation is a vital resource for educating developers about the most prominent Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) platform in the open-source community. Although CI/CD accelerates the software development process, it poses a significant risk to the software supply chain, as demonstrated by recurring attacks on open-source GitHub Actions dependencies and workflows. While previous work has prioritized detecting vulnerable CI/CD workflows, we assess, from a preventive perspective, whether the official documentation provides security guidance for secure CI/CD. In this work, we extract 459 security advice items from the GitHub documentation using a Large Language Model-based few-shot approach. We then apply the SAcoding methodology to the OWASP Top 10 CI/CD security risk framework to identify actionable recommendations. GitHub and OWASP align on credential and configuration-based weaknesses; however GitHub does not effectively utilize its visual alerts to inform developers.

title: Making Binary Decisions in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations.
abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) is a digital organization governed by rules encoded in smart contracts on a blockchain [1], [2]. In recent years, DAOs have evolved into large-scale entities with thousands of pseudo-anonymous members. The members coordinate and make collective decisions without a centralized authority.

title: Automated Resilience Assessment for Autonomous Systems Using System-on-Chip Architectures.
abstract: In autonomous systems, consolidating hardware onto System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms provides size, weight, and power advantages, yet creates new attack surfaces where a single component’s compromise can propagate attacks across the shared bus to other safety-critical functions. Existing SoC security analyses focus on implementing access controls and system-level anomaly detection algorithms, but lack systematic methods for evaluating how these architectures degrade when compromised. This research introduces an automated resilience assessment that takes an SoC architecture model with pre-assigned security features and systematically generates component failure and compromise scenarios, computes structural and firewall-aware blast radii (the set of components reachable from a compromised node), detects single points of failure (SPOFs), quantifies risk amplification factors based on the blast radii, and enumerates multi-hop attack paths to safety-critical targets. The assessment is formulated in Answer Set Programming (ASP). It is evaluated on two case studies: an 8-component SoC drone and an 11-component DARPA Cyber Assured Systems Engineering (CASE) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The assessment runs in under 15 seconds for the 8-component architecture and under 30 seconds for the CASE UAV, for these two case studies. Results show that topology-driven weaknesses (policy server concentration, common-mode bus failures, and single-string service chains) persist across distinctly different security architectures, suggesting that some weaknesses cannot be removed by per-component hardening alone. The accompanying formal metric definitions enable systematic comparison across architectures and security postures.

title: Behavior-Guided Decompilation of AVR Firmware with Autonomous LLM Agents : Paper Type: Practical Experience Report.
abstract: Legacy embedded firmware represents a critical security risk in modern infrastructure, yet traditional decompilation tools struggle with hardware-coupled code. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in decompiling desktop software, their application to bare-metal firmware remains unexplored. We present a behavior-guided reverse engineering framework employing autonomous LLM agents that perform multi-step reasoning: reading disassembly, consulting MCU documentation, generating candidate code, compiling, simulating, analyzing trace differentials, and iteratively refining solutions across multiple attempts. This agentic approach, fundamentally different from single-shot API queries, enables the model to reason about complex firmware through tool use and self-correction. Using cycle-accurate simulation as our behavioral oracle, we evaluate two frontier coding agents, Claude Code (Opus 4.5) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.1-codex-max), across 52 real-world AVR firmware projects. Claude achieves a 54.4% metric-level pass rate compared to Codex’s 37.0%, winning 41 of 52 head-to-head comparisons. Despite this, both agents exhibit systematic failures in safety-critical constructs: volatile qualifiers, interrupt handlers, and Harvard architecture memory access. Our findings reveal a critical "safety gap" where high syntactic accuracy masks deep behavioral flaws, demonstrating the need for human oversight and hardware-in-the-loop verification for firmware decompilation. While our empirical study focuses on the AVR architecture, the methodology generalizes to other embedded platforms and is the subject of ongoing work.

title: Balancing Mutation Entropy and Session Continuity in SDN-Based Moving Target Defense.
abstract: Moving Target Defense (MTD) improves system resilience by dynamically mutating exposed network attributes such as IP addresses and ports. However, frequent mutation can disrupt active TCP and UDP sessions, resulting in increased latency and degraded quality of service in modern networked applications. This work presents Continuity-Preserving Address Mutation (CPAM), an SDN-based mechanism that balances mutation entropy with session continuity. CPAM decouples primary virtual IP (VIP) rotation from session-bound mappings by retaining VIP bindings for active flows while assigning new VIPs to incoming connections. This design enables periodic address mutation without interrupting ongoing sessions. We implement CPAM in a Mininet-based SDN testbed and evaluate its impact on network performance and controller overhead. Experimental results show that CPAM maintains latency comparable to a traditional network$(\approx 0.168 \text{ms}$RTT), preserves stable TCP throughput during mutation events, and introduces negligible control-plane overhead. These results demonstrate that sessionaware VIP rotation can retain the security benefits of MTD while maintaining transport-layer stability.

title: One Error to Rule Them All: Can a Single Bit-Flip Disrupt Fully Homomorphic Encryption?
abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without decryption, representing a major advance in privacy-preserving technologies. This capability is especially valuable for safety-critical domains such as healthcare, finance, and government, where sensitive data must remain protected while enabling third-party computations. Despite its importance, systematic studies of FHE’s resilience—a critical concern for high-reliability applications—remain largely unexplored.In this work, we investigate the resilience of CKKS (Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song), a widely used FHE scheme that supports approximate arithmetic for privacy-preserving machine learning and scientific simulations. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of CKKS under single-bit and multi-bit hardware errors, focusing on how Residue Number System (RNS) and Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) optimizations affect (worsen) error propagation. Across over 175 million error-injection experiments spanning 500 parameter configurations, we identify error-resilience patterns that are general, data-independent, and consistent across FHE pipeline variations. Our findings offer a foundation for further work in designing fault-tolerant cryptographic systems.

title: LLM-Empowered Discovery of Windows APIs Exploitable for Persistent Storage in Fileless Attacks.
abstract: Fileless attacks have gained significant traction recently due to their minimal footprint and substantial real-world consequences. However, existing methods often trigger detection by antivirus tools when storing malicious content directly in the file systems. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to achieve persistent storage in fileless attacks. This method leverages legitimate Windows Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to store malicious code either outside the conventional file system or indirectly within it. We established criteria for exploitable APIs and employed ChatGPT for an automated rule-based assessment on 9,410 publicly disclosed Windows APIs. Out of the 80 APIs deemed exploitable, manual verification substantiated the effectiveness of 64, indicating an automation precision rate of 80%. This demonstrates the efficiency of using ChatGPT for automated identification of exploitable Windows APIs. Remarkably, 54 of the 64 APIs are previously unreported for fileless attacks and are typically used in benign programs, posing a challenge in terms of false positives for antivirus software to detect or blacklist them. We developed a malware program using each exploitable API to store and retrieve existing malicious code. During both static and dynamic detection phases, 37 of 64 malware programs successfully circumvented mainstream antivirus solutions. This underscores the efficacy of our persistent storage method in bypassing both static and dynamic detection systems, enabling the storage of arbitrary malicious code on compromised devices. We have communicated our findings to pertinent security vendors and also made the source code for specific Proof of Concepts (PoCs) of the exploitable APIs publicly available.

title: Ruby: Unmasking Unsafe Rust in Stripped Binaries via Machine Learning.
abstract: Rust, as an emerging system programming language, introduces unsafe to allow developers to bypass safety checks during compilation. As a result, memory safety bugs are typically confined to the unsafe regions, which have been the primary focus of Rust bug-finding tools. However, such tools rely on the presence of the unsafe keyword in Rust source code; there are no tools available that can examine Rust binaries to pinpoint unsafe areas. Therefore, we propose Ruby, the first tool that unmasks unsafe regions in Rust binaries using machine learning. By capturing the subtle differences in the binary instructions, Ruby can identify 91.75% of the total unsafe regions with a false positive rate of 6.16%, beating SOTA LLM models including GPT-5.2, Claude-4.5 and Gemini-3. We further applied Ruby to guide symbolic execution and fuzzing, showing a speed-up of 57.95% and 21.26%, with five bugs confirmed and patched by Google in Android library fuzzing.

title: Robust and Automated Reconfiguration of Byzantine Wide-Area Replication.
abstract: Distributed systems handle adversarial nodes through redundancy, which imposes a significant performance overhead. In blockchain systems, Byzantine fault-tolerant state-machine replication (BFT-SMR) is the replicated service that totally orders client transactions before execution. While prior research has primarily focused on designing novel consensus algorithms with improved performance, recent studies have shown that further gains can be achieved through configuration optimization. More precisely, replicas can monitor network latency to dynamically assign the leader role and tune voting weights, thereby improving consensus performance. However, we identify three vulnerabilities in this process that Byzantine nodes can exploit. To address these weaknesses, we propose Beware, a reconfiguration framework that filters out falsified latency reports, computes robust weight distributions, and applies machine learning to converge towards Byzantine-resilient configurations. Our evaluation shows that Beware reduces consensus latency by up to 45% compared to existing solutions.

title: A Secure, Manifest-Based Framework for Delegated Privilege Promotion.
abstract: Large-scale enterprise software systems commonly run as unprivileged service accounts to enforce least privilege, yet still depend on a small set of privileged components -- such as executables with elevated ownership, permissions, or capabilities -- for narrowly scoped operations. This creates a persistent security and operational conflict during maintenance. Automated patching tools running without elevated privileges cannot safely update privileged components without either executing the entire patch with full administrative rights or requiring manual administrator intervention. We present a secure, manifest-based infrastructure for delegated promotion of privileged software components, deployed in production as part of a large-scale enterprise database system serving both cloud and on-premises installations. The design centers on a minimal privileged mediator that validates cryptographically protected metadata and allows an unprivileged process to promote only vendor-approved files. The system explicitly mitigates Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) attacks using file-descriptor-bound validation and promotion, supports offline key rotation and revocation, and enables zero-downtime self-update via atomic replacement.

title: Resilience Assessment of AI Accelerators: A Driver-Level Fault Injection Methodology.
abstract: In this proposal, we present a driver-level fault injection for AI resilience assessment as a complementary and cross-layer methodology compared to the state of the art.

title: Mind the Driver: A Fault Injection Methodology for AI Systems.
abstract: Current AI systems reliability assessment is fragmented across abstraction layers, with existing methods focusing either on low-level hardware faults or high-level software perturbations while largely overlooking the driver interface. We propose driver-level fault injection as a cross-layer methodology that targets this hardware-software boundary, capturing soft errors, hardware anomalies, and system-level instabilities for a more holistic resilience assessment.

title: A Configurable Logic Architecture Based on Micro-Electromechanical Relays for Nuclear Power Safety Systems.
abstract: Electro-mechanical relays are a key component used in Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) safety critical systems. However, Electro-mechanical relays (at the macro-scale) have reliability and maintenance issues, excessive heat dissipation, and large area footprint which tend to limit their use in smaller advanced reactors. In contrast, a configurable architecture built entirely from micro-electromechanical (MEMs) or Nano-electromechanical relays (NEMs) has the potential to effectively eliminate leakage energy losses, operate at high temperatures (175 °C and above) and tolerate radiation doses in excess of 100 Mrad. Motivated by these challenges, this paper presents a novel configurable micro-scale relay architecture that drastically reduces the size of relays [1], enabling thousands of logic functions on a single chip. The proposed architecture provides a foundation for a technology-diverse, low-complexity, radiation-and transienthardened logic architecture suitable for Safety Actuation and Protection Systems in extreme environments [1]–[3].

title: Thinking Inside the Box: Injecting Realistic Radiation Faults in ML Accelerators.
abstract: Machine Learning accelerators are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications such as autonomous vehicles and space environments, where exposure to radiation poses serious reliability risks. To evaluate and mitigate this risk, we test tensor processing units (TPUs) with neutron, proton, and heavy-ion beams that account for 104 million years of natural exposure on the Earth, and more than 1,000 years of mission in outer space, showing that, contrasting with conventional single-bit models, faults affect localized rectangular regions of tensor outputs. We then build TPU-FI, an experimentally-tuned software-based fault-injector, predicting TPUs failure-in-time rates within, on average, 1.7x of beam results. Through 6 million software fault injections, we analyze how fault type, model architecture, layer type, and input data affect prediction correctness, finding that fully connected and convolutional layers exhibit higher vulnerability and different inputs trigger distinct fault propagation paths, especially in attention-based models.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: What Makes Software Bugs Escape Testing? Evidence from a Large-Scale Empirical Study.
abstract: Understanding how software defects manifest and evolve in production environments is critical for improving reliability. While previous research has largely focused on pre-release defects, the nature of residual faults, i.e., those escaping testing and surfacing post-release, remains poorly understood. This paper presents a large-scale characterization of pre- and post-release defects across C/C++ and Java systems, encompassing over 14k defects mined from open-source projects. We employ a broad suite of software metrics to capture diverse code attributes such as complexity, size, structure, and development history.Results show that post-release defects are concentrated in older, frequently modified, and high-churn components, typically requiring longer and more complex fixes than pre-release ones. These findings highlight that residual defects arise more from evolutionary and process dynamics than code structure alone, suggesting that reliability engineering should prioritize targeted testing in mature and complex code regions.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Praxis: Integrating Program Analysis with Observability for Root-Cause Analysis.
abstract: Unresolved production cloud incidents cost an average of over $2M per hour. This paper introduces PRAXIS, an orchestrator that manages and deploys an agentic workflow for diagnosing code- and configuration-caused cloud incidents. PRAXIS employs an LLM-driven structured traversal over two types of graph: (1) a service dependency graph (SDG) that captures microservice-level dependencies; and (2) a hammock-block program dependence graph (PDG) that captures code-level dependencies for each microservice. Compared to state-of-the-art ReAct baselines, PRAXIS improves RCA accuracy by up to 6.3x while reducing token consumption by 5.3x. PRAXIS is demonstrated on a set of 30 comprehensive real-world incidents that is being compiled into an RCA benchmark.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Efficient Bug Detection by Inferring Implicit API Contract of Pointer State Transition.
abstract: Modern C functions heavily rely on implicit API contracts—assumptions about pointer validity that are contingent on execution paths. Violations of these unstated rules, such as dereferencing NULL pointers after failed operations, remain a primary source of reliability bugs. Unfortunately, traditional whole-program analyses and contract-mining techniques fail to effectively capture such implicit semantics. We present ConTract, a compositional framework that automatically infers and checks contracts governing pointer state transitions. ConTract models function behaviors as state transition systems over abstract pointer resources, synthesizing precise state preconditions and postconditions. This approach enables efficient inter-procedural consistency checking without redundant path exploration. Built atop Clang and applied to diverse real-world C software, ConTract uncovered 209 previously unrecognized pointer-semantic inconsistencies. To date, developers have confirmed 127 reports, with 28 fixed and 2 CVEs assigned.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: RESIST: $\underline{\text{Res}}$ilience Against $\underline{\mathrm{S}}$ilent $\underline{\mathrm{S}}$ilicon $\underline{\mathrm{T}}$hreats - A Cross-Layer Perspective (Tutorial).
abstract: As process nodes shrink and datacenters scale toward exascale, Silent Data Corruptions (SDCs) resulting from underlying hardware defects have emerged as a primary challenge to integrity at-scale. SDCs have resulted in a wide variety of failures, such as corrupted model weights during AI training, silent database corruptions, and poor recommendations, among many others. This tutorial provides a comprehensive journey through the SDC landscape, led by academic and industry experts. Our discussion begins at the silicon level, examining the physics of the silicon defects at the root of these corruptions. We then move up the stack to understand the role of architectural decisions in reducing SDCs, evaluating the trade-offs posed by various architectural designs and reliability mitigations. Next, we will examine the role software plays in mitigating defects. A key focus here will be the testing lifecycle – exploring how machines are tested before use and continuously screened within a hyperscaler's fleet – as well as how to add software-level resiliency when faults do occur. Finally, we will discuss workload-level behaviors, examining the inherent resilience (or lack thereof) in distributed systems and large-scale AI training and inference. Participants will leave with a clear understanding of open research questions that will define the next decade of reliable systems design.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Measuring Attack Observability in Cloud Telemetry Logs: A Cross-Platform Analysis.
abstract: With unparalleled flexibility in management and resource scaling, cloud computing is widely adopted and growing. Cyber threats targeting cloud instances require security solutions as much as physical infrastructures. Although traditional host-based and network-based security tools can be deployed to detect malicious activities within a cloud instance, they are not suitable for monitoring activities specific to cloud environments such as cloud resource management and authentication.In this paper, we systematically investigate the effectiveness of cloud telemetry logs, for cybersecurity monitoring and defense. While cloud infrastructures provide telemetry logs to help cloud users and administrators monitor various activities such as performance or resource management, there remains limited understanding of the extent to which these logs capture evidence of attacks, the types of attacks they can reveal, and their effectiveness across platforms. To address this gap, we conduct 35 attacks categorized under the MITRE ATT&CK framework on three major cloud infrastructures, and collect telemetry logs under both control and attack scenarios. Through differential analysis, we identify which log fields are impacted by specific attacks, assess platform-level consistency, and characterize gaps in log observability. Our new findings show that default telemetry configurations reflect 45∼48% of the attacks, while enabling extended logging increases this to 65∼88%, depending on the platform. We also evaluate the cost-effectiveness and performance overhead of telemetry logs, demonstrating minimal deployment costs to enable the extended logging.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Understanding and Exploiting DNS Relaying: Harnessing Legitimate Services for DNS Attacks.
abstract: We introduce a novel technique, DNS relaying, exploiting the fact that many services (CDNs, web/email servers) perform DNS lookups for arbitrary hostnames from untrusted clients. Consequently, DNS relaying turns legitimate services into intermediaries, relaying attacker-originated messages via DNS requests to (internal) resolvers and, ultimately, to target nameservers. Our investigation reveals the root causes of this behavior across various services, including request routing, domain ownership verification, sender tracking, user experience enhancements, and security inspections. Importantly, we uncover a new response-latency covert channel that enables bi-directional communication over these DNS relays. By exploiting benign services as relays, DNS relaying circumvents modern security perimeters and amplifies the impact of DNS attacks. We demonstrate that DNS relaying enhances three legacy DNS attacks by enabling relayed DNS tunneling to bypass edge security, relayed DNS amplification, and relayed DNS exploit to reach otherwise inaccessible DNS servers and clients. Our Internet-wide measurement shows that relayed DNS tunneling can achieve 1,400 bits/request exfiltration and 6 bits/request infiltration; relayed DNS amplification can reach a 535-times packet amplification factor; and DNS relaying expands the DNS exploit attack surface by 8 times in terms of reachable server IPs. We responsibly disclosed our findings to 15 major vendors, receiving acknowledgments from multiple parties. The most affected vendor, Akamai, specifically recognized DNS relaying as a security threat due to our discovered practical infiltration channel.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Meta-Architecture Binary Code Analysis.
abstract: Recent work has applied deep learning to binary code analysis, enabling more efficient and accurate analysis. However, deep learning–based binary analysis faces two major challenges. First, training such models requires large datasets, which are unavailable for many instruction set architectures (ISAs). Second, the diversity of ISAs creates substantial overhead, as building models for each ISA demands time and effort.To address these challenges, we propose meta-architecture binary code analysis, in which a model trained on a data-rich ISA can be reused for other ISAs without modification. Our key insight is that intermediate representations (IRs) can abstract away ISA-specific differences. By analyzing IR, our approach learns knowledge that is transferable across ISAs, enabling practical meta-architecture analysis. We demonstrate this idea through two tasks: malware detection and function similarity detection. An extensive evaluation across four ISAs (x86, ARM, MIPS, and PowerPC) shows strong transferability and high performance across diverse binary analysis tasks.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: PDLogger: Automatic Multi-log Generation for Practical Software Development.
abstract: Logging is indispensable for maintaining the reliability and diagnosability of modern software, yet developers still struggle to log effectively. Existing automated logging techniques focus on generating logs in a single-log scenario, predicting a single log within a method, and therefore cannot produce complete, high-quality log statements that accurately reflect real-world practice, where multiple logs often appear within one method. They also neglect deeper semantic dependencies among methods and consider only a narrow set of candidate variables, leading to superficial or incomplete logs. In this paper, we present PDLogger, the first end-to-end log generation technique expressly designed for practical, multi-log scenarios. PDLogger operates in three phases. (1) Log position prediction: block-type–based prompts guide a large language model (LLM) to suggest candidate positions across four types of blocks of a method. (2) Log generation: semantic dependency analysis and function-aware variable analysis enable PDLogger to generate logs that capture the root cause and to supply member and non-member functions, along with their expressions, as variable candidates. (3) Log refinement: level refinement and context-sensitive deduplication prune false positives and redundant logs. We evaluate PDLogger on 14,370 log statements drawn from 10 widely used Java projects. Compared to the state-of-the-art, PDLogger achieves an average improvement of 64.8% in log-position F1-score, 51.4% in level accuracy, 31.5% in variable F1-score, and 36.4% in message quality (BERTScore).
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Dependable Real-Time Guarantees in Converged 5G and Time-Sensitive Networks.
abstract: Ongoing standardization efforts in 5G and Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) aim to provide safety-critical applications with real-time communication. However, network schedules often rely on idealistic delay models that can jeopardize the validity of their guarantees. For instance, we identified scenarios where a 99.99% reliability in the inner 5G network diminishes to below 10% when looking at the end-to-end guarantees in TSN. Moreover, 5G-TSN networks remain prone to abrupt delay outliers (e.g., due to 5G line-of-sight blockage) that are difficult to predict and often do not leave enough time to reactively reconfigure the network. To overcome these challenges, we introduced Full Interleaving Packet Scheduling (FIPS) as, to the best of our knowledge, the first wireless-friendly IEEE 802.1Qbv scheduler that provides probabilistic end-to-end latency guarantees by utilizing 5G packet delay histograms. We extended this work with an$(m, k)$-firm Elevation Policy that acts as a fallback to the primary scheduler (e.g., FIPS) to uphold weakly hard real-time guarantees under network conditions that are not captured by the 5G histograms. Our work thereby makes a substantial advance towards dependable QoS guarantees in networks with probabilistic delay characteristics and abrupt delay outliers.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: An (m, k)-firm Elevation Policy for Weakly Hard Real-Time in Converged 5G-TSN Networks.
abstract: Ongoing standardization efforts in 5G and Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) aim to provide safety-critical applications with real-time communication. However, 5G-TSN network schedules often rely on idealistic delay models that can jeopardize the validity of their guarantees. This paper presents an (m, k)-firm Elevation Policy to uphold a base level of weakly hard real-time guarantees (WHRT). It augments the primary schedule with a dynamic priority-driven scheme to elevate the priority of m out of k consecutive frames if they experience unexpected delays. Our evaluations demonstrate the necessity of WHRT to increase fault-tolerance against 5G delay outliers and to uphold the quality of control within a 5G-TSN networked control system. Still, only a small resource overhead is imposed during epochs where the primary schedule is valid and can serve stronger QoS guarantees. The (m, k)-firm Elevation Policy thereby yields a robust but lightweight fallback mechanism to serve applications with dependable guarantees during unstable network conditions.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: [Tutorial] Securing Your Airspace: The Interplay Between Cybersecurity, Sensing, and Safety.
abstract: This tutorial examines modern airspace monitoring technologies and their cybersecurity implications. We cover sensing approaches ranging from traditional radar to passive techniques using ambient radio-frequency (RF) signals, discuss threats such as spoofing and adversarial evasion targeting sensing infrastructure, and share insights from our deployed passive sensing system, along with open research directions.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: PeerLumen: A Bitcoin P2P Honeypot Telescope.
abstract: Bitcoin's peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture enables open participation but exposes the network to evolving threats, making timely anomaly detection essential but arduous. Existing approaches rely on passive detection and miss early malicious activities. This paper presents PeerLumen, a client-side honeypot telescope designed for active and continuous anomaly detection in the Bitcoin P2P network, with the capability to monitor and analyze peer activities across IPv4, IPv6, and Tor onion networks. PeerLumen emulates legitimate node behavior and proactively interacts with live peers to unveil deviations that are opaque to passive monitors. The system incorporates entropy-driven behavioral metrics to identify anomalies arising from both individual nodes and coordinated activities across multiple nodes. The deployment and the corresponding experiments on the Bitcoin mainnet show that PeerLumen can effectively discover blockchain forks, shadow IPs, and port-proliferation behaviors. These findings demonstrate that PeerLumen can serve as an active-measurement instrument, significantly improving visibility into adversarial dynamics in decentralized P2P systems. As the first tool of its kind in this area, PeerLumen can also serve as a baseline for future research.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: From Security Standards to Adversary Emulation: An AI-Assisted Framework for ICS Security Assessment.
abstract: Security assessments are essential to ensure that Industrial Control Systems (ICS) comply with cybersecurity standards and remain resilient to evolving cyber threats. While standards such as IEC 62443 and NIST provide structured guidance for securing industrial systems, translating these highlevel requirements into concrete and executable security tests remains a largely manual process. In practice, analysts must interpret heterogeneous standards, derive security controls, identify relevant adversarial behaviors, and design testing procedures for the target environment. This limits the repeatability and scalability of security assessments across industrial contexts. This paper presents a standards-driven approach that transforms cybersecurity requirements into executable adversary emulation procedures for ICS security assessment. The proposed framework extracts security controls from standards, aligns them with adversarial behaviors described in the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base for ICS, and generates environment-aware test actions executable through the MITRE CALDERA adversary emulation platform. An AIassisted pipeline supports the interpretation of requirements and the generation of test procedures while preserving human oversight and process traceability. By leveraging CALDERA as the execution layer, the approach decouples the assessment methodology from the target system, enabling the same adversary procedures to be applied across different environments such as virtual testbeds, digital twins, and operational systems. The approach is validated through two industrial case studies, demonstrating how standards-driven adversary emulation supports repeatable security assessments in heterogeneous ICS environments.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: AnBridge: Protecting On-Device AI with Android Virtualization Framework.
abstract: When deployed on-device, AI gets exposed to device-based attacks. To mitigate this threat, Android recently introduced the Android Virtualization Framework (AVF), enabling the creation of protected virtual machines (pVMs).However, the code running in the pVM is subject to a new programming model, making the porting of existing AI code in the pVM hard without a significant rearchitecting.In this paper, we propose a new pVM programming model, and a related communication middleware, to simplify the migration of existing Android on-device AI code into pVMs. We evaluate the performance of our solution in terms of both latency and throughput, including workloads that access peripheral devices. Our results show modest overheads (2-14%) when pVM-resident native code invokes high-level Java functions running on the host. Finally, we discuss the practical deployment of our solution by applying it to two AI security-sensitive Android applications.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: MBA-Sniffer: Rapidly Locating Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic Obfuscation in Binary Code.
abstract: Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) is a promising obfuscation method that transforms code into complex but equivalent constructs that blend arithmetic and bitwise computation. Numerous research works have been proposed to reverse MBA obfuscation. However, they share a common assumption: the location of MBA obfuscation must already be known by manual analysis. We observe that the assumption actually does not hold in real-world deobfuscation and identifying precise boundaries of MBA obfuscation is never a trivial task.In this paper, we propose a dynamic, trace-based blackbox solution to pinpoint MBA obfuscation at the binary level. We design a novel Lower-Bound-First sliding window strategy and directed input/output sampling to efficiently locate and verify the promising instruction sequences that may include MBA obfuscation. Unlike earlier approaches, our technique stands out by capturing the core principle of MBA obfuscation: using a complex calculation to produce the same result as a simple computation. In comparative experiments against four state-of-the-art methods across three real-world evaluation sets obfuscated with over 1400 MBA expressions, our prototype MBA-Sniffer exhibits superior performance in terms of correctness and completeness.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: From MIRAGE to CLEAR: Component-Level Explainable Anomaly Reasoning for Autonomous Vehicle Perception Systems.
abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) perception systems remain vulnerable to failures that current anomaly detectors can flag but cannot trace to a specific component; an attribution gap that impedes forensics and emerging transparency mandates like the EU AI Act. We introduce a unified framework comprising MIRAGE and CLEAR. MIRAGE (MUTCD-Informed Realistic Anomalous Generation Engine) integrates 48,022 real-world driving scenes from nuScenes, Waymo Open, and Argoverse 2 with structured rules from the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), generating 5,847 annotated anomalous scenarios with known module-level ground truth across four violation types: direct, subtle, contextual, and environmental. This data powers CLEAR, a hierarchical three-layer LLM pipeline that detects anomalies, classifies violations, and attributes failures to Traffic Sign Recognition (TSR), Automated Lane Centering (ALC), or Object Detection (OD) with interpretable justifications. Confidence-gated propagation and schema-constrained outputs prevent error cascades and minimize hallucinations. CLEAR achieves 95.2% detection accuracy, 62.3% classification accuracy, and 84% attribution accuracy on direct TSR violations. A Top-2 evaluation paired with per-module confidence analysis raises overall attribution to 74.6%, confirming that apparent misattributions largely reflect the multi-module nature of anomaly types rather than reasoning failures. These results show that grounding LLM reasoning in structured traffic regulations enables reliable, interpretable forensics for AV perception systems, offering a practical path toward auditable, regulation-compliant safety analysis. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/David-FR/MIRAGE_CLEAR.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Towards Automated Detection of Latent Software Robustness Failures Using Large Language Models.
abstract: Robustness failures occur when a system deviates from its specification under invalid inputs or stressful environmental conditions. Automated detection of these failures poses a substantial challenge, especially in the face of incomplete specifications and latent failure modes that do not produce explicit indicators. In this work, we propose the development of an approach for the automated detection of latent robustness failures in software systems by leveraging the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). In particular, we define a pipeline that integrates multiple stages of robustness assessment, including enhancement of specifications, testing, and analysis of system behaviors, enabling a holistic and scalable approach.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Trust, but Verify: ByzTwin-Range, a Digital Twin Cyber-Range for Byzantine Faults.
abstract: Critical infrastructures increasingly rely on interconnected and software-driven Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), exposing operational processes to both accidental failures and sophisticated adversarial behavior. While Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) protocols offer robustness against arbitrary faults, evaluating their behavior under realistic cyber-physical conditions remains challenging: traditional cyber ranges lack timing fidelity, and testing in production environments is unsafe. This paper introduces ByzTwin-Range, a dual-layer architecture that integrates a production-grade BFT deployment with a Digital Twin (DT) to enable controlled experimentation, stress testing, and Byzantine fault injection using live operational data. The DT mirrors real system state, executes "What-if" analyses through co-simulation and emulation, and identifies synchrony vulnerabilities, i.e., misconfigured timeouts, timing-sensitive false suspicions, and adversarial delay exploits, configuration weaknesses, and adversarial behaviors that may undermine BFT guarantees. Insights from the twin are fed back into the operational deployment through a secure advisory channel, supporting continuous validation and adaptive hardening. The proposed design leverages industry-standard technologies (Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture, Time-Sensitive Networking, Functional Mock-up Unit/High-Level Architecture, QUIC/mutual TLS) to maximize feasibility and compatibility with existing industrial workflows. ByzTwin-Range establishes a practical foundation for next-generation, BFT-aware cyber ranges and paves the way for more resilient CPSs through continuous testing, differential-privacy-enabled analytics, and future proof-of-concept implementations.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Cross-Referencing Whitepaper Claims and Smart Contract Code for Automated ICO Auditing.
abstract: Initial Coin Offering (ICO) whitepapers serve as informal specifications for token-governing smart contracts, yet no existing tool verifies whether deployed code matches the claims in these documents. NLP-based fraud detection analyzes whitepaper text but ignores the contract. Smart contract analysis tools examine code but have no knowledge of what developers promised. We built ICOAudit, a pipeline that bridges this gap. ICOAudit extracts structured claims from ICO whitepapers using LLM-based information extraction across nine token-governance categories, analyzes the corresponding Ethereum smart contracts via Slither static analysis, and checks each claim against code-level features using a hybrid rule-based and LLM-based consistency scorer. We evaluate ICOAudit on a novel paired dataset of 60 real Ethereum ICOs with whitepaper text, verified contract source, and fraud labels. The pipeline detected 86 specification-implementation inconsistencies across 21 of 54 analyzed projects. Fraud-labeled projects exhibited$\mathbf{3. 0} \times$higher combined inconsistency signals than legitimate ones$(p=0.075$, suggestive but below the 0.05 significance threshold), while text-only analysis showed no discrimination$(p=0.569)$. The five highest-severity inconsistencies, where entire promised subsystems were absent from deployed code, all involved confirmed fraud cases. Claim extraction validated against hand-labeled ground truth from Cohney et al. achieved$\mathbf{F} \mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0. 7 2}$across$\mathbf{1 9}$ICOs.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: MeshGuard: MUD-Based Network Access Control for Large-Scale Thread-Powered IoT Networks.
abstract: The IETF standard Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) enables manufacturers to equip IoT devices with certified URLs that provide traffic profiles for those devices, helping administrators enforce network access control. However, MUD assumes devices operate on full IP stacks and therefore does not account for constrained IoT devices running Thread--the dominant low-power mesh networking standard--which lacks complete TCP/IP functionality. While prior work proposes extensions to support MUD in Thread environments, these approaches are limited to simple topologies with a single border router and do not scale to realistic deployments with multiple, heterogeneous border routers. We introduce MeshGuard, a framework enabling MUD-based access control in complex Thread networks, with any number of border routers. MeshGuard extends the Mesh Link Establishment (MLE) protocol to deliver MUD information from constrained devices to border routers regardless of network topology. Moreover, MeshGuard leverages Software-Defined Networking (SDN) to synchronize access control lists across all routers. Experiments on our proof-of-concept with real devices (nRF5340, nRF52833, Raspberry-Pi 3) demonstrate enhanced security, minimal overhead, and linear scalability compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Edge-Based Privacy Auditing for Trustworthy Humanoid Robot Interaction.
abstract: The deployment of humanoid robots in domestic and care environments introduces a “Privacy-Anthropomorphism Paradox”: the very social cues designed to foster trust and user acceptance can inadvertently lower privacy guardrails, encouraging users to disclose sensitive information to multi-modal sensing platforms. To address this challenge, we propose RoboAudit, an edge-based framework for real-time privacy awareness and mitigation in humanoid robot interaction. RoboAudit integrates three complementary mechanisms: (1) Observational Privacy Auditing, which detects potential privacy exposures in robot perception and learning pipelines without requiring model retraining; (2) Privacy Topography, a context-aware navigation strategy that applies semantic scrubbing to avoid or minimize sensing in privacy-sensitive zones; and (3) Anthropomorphic Transparency, which leverages social gaze and behavioral cues to communicate privacy and security states to users in an intuitive manner.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: [Tutorial] Confidential Computing: Fundamentals, Platforms, and Research.
abstract: Confidential Computing (CC) has emerged as a critical security paradigm for protecting sensitive code and data within untrusted public compute infrastructures. This tutorial provides a comprehensive, top-down exploration of the CC landscape, organized into three sections: Fundamentals, Platforms, and Research.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Moving Target Defense in Cyber-Physical Systems.
abstract: Cyber-physical power systems face coordinated false data injection attack (FDI) attacks that exploit the cyber measurement pipeline and knowledge of the power-flow Jacobian to bypass bad-data detection. Existing moving target defense (MTD) approaches address each layer in isolation, leaving a critical cross-layer seam that adaptive adversaries can exploit. This paper presents a unified, agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework that jointly optimizes physical MTD actions such as topology switching, flexible alternating current transmission system (FACTS) configuration, and distributed energy resource (DER) control with measurementcentric cyber-agility actions, including dynamic watermarking, adaptive scheduling, and estimator reconfiguration. A large language model (LLM) orchestrator, grounded via retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over domain threat knowledge, guides a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) network operating over a high-fidelity digital twin with crosslayer interdependency modeling. Preliminary results on the IEEE 14-bus system demonstrate improved FDI detection over physical-only and cyber-only baselines while maintaining frequency deviation within$\pm 0.05 \text{Hz}$, with full evaluation planned across IEEE 14, 39, 57, and 118-bus benchmarks.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: VeriExist: Blockchain-Assisted Existence-Verifiable Protocol in User-Centric Data Sharing.
abstract: User-centric data sharing is increasingly adopted to meet stringent privacy and compliance requirements (e.g., GDPR). However, this paradigm introduces the critical vulnerability of selective disclosure: driven by self-interest, data owners possess a natural motive to maliciously conceal unfavorable records, such as hiding medical histories to commit insurance fraud. Existing encryption search and blockchainassisted solutions ensure the correctness of search results but fail to guarantee data completeness, leaving a loophole for owners to manipulate state or hide cryptographic keys. In this paper, we propose VeriExist, a blockchain-assisted protocol that establishes existence verifiability as a fundamental dependability property in user-centric data sharing. VeriExist utilizes a novel duallayer key index on the blockchain-comprising a pre-filled sorted keyword layer and a sequential state/epoch layer. This architecture strictly deprives owners of the ability to hide data while preventing neighbor-keyword leakage during proofs of absence. To ensure scalability, we introduce an enhanced encryption search mechanism featuring tree-based key derivation and epoch-based parallel search, coupled with an on-chain/off-chain collaborative architecture. Comprehensive evaluations using OpenMRS, a complex medical open-source benchmark deployed on Hyperledger Fabric, demonstrate that VeriExist achieves robust data existence verification with negligible user-perceived latency and exhibits superior blockchain scalability compared to state-of-theart solutions.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: LLM-PEA: Leveraging Large Language Models Against Phishing Email Attacks.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed inside email-security pipelines, raising the question of how they behave not just on benign messages but on adversarially crafted phishing content. We present LLM-PEA, an evaluation framework that probes GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4, and Grok-3 under three prompting strategies (structured, zero-shot, chain-of-thought) across a clean baseline and three attack dimensions: adversarial rephrasing, prompt injection, and cross-lingual translation. The three models attain 95%, 94%, and 88% accuracy on the balanced baseline, but susceptibility depends on the attack. Adversarial rephrasing of 189 matched phishing samples yields attack success rates of 4.2% (GPT-4o), 12.7% (Claude Sonnet 4), and 0% (Grok-3); a separate single-template instruction-override on 1,000 original emails yields 4.2%, 1.3%, and 12.3% respectively—a different susceptibility ordering. Applying six injection templates to the same 189 rephrased samples yields 1.1%, 2.9%, and 1.6%, together with the adversarial-only results covering three of four cells of a 2×2 factorial on matched inputs. The sharpest degradation is cross-lingual: Claude Sonnet 4’s false-positive rate rises from 2.4% in English to a mean of 24.1% across Bangla, Chinese, and Hindi (a +904% relative increase), peaking at 30.6% in Bangla and erasing its baseline advantage. All runs use temperature 0; adversarial rephrases are generated by GPT-4o, itself one of the evaluated detectors. No single model is uniformly robust across these three attack dimensions.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Color Matters: Trigger Color Affects Success in Federated Backdoor Attacks.
abstract: Federated learning is vulnerable to backdoor attacks in which malicious clients inject poisoned updates while preserving benign-task performance. In this paper, we study a semantics-driven backdoor mechanism in which attackers use natural visual accessories as triggers and manipulate only the trigger color while keeping the attack pipeline fixed. Our framework considers semantic trigger objects such as masks and sunglasses, instantiated in black and white variants, and evaluates their effect in a controlled federated learning setting. Malicious clients construct poisoned samples by applying a trigger to source-class images and relabeling them to an attacker-chosen target class, while benign clients train only on clean data. We analyze this mechanism under both a standard poisoning objective and a stronger SABLE-based objective that combines clean classification loss, triggered target loss, feature-separation loss in the penultimate representation space, and regularization to keep malicious updates close to the global model. This design enables the attack to remain effective while reducing excessive update drift. Experiments on a four-class CelebA hair-color task show that trigger color significantly changes attack success rate even when trigger semantics, placement, and poisoning budget are unchanged. White triggers are more effective for attacks targeting the blond class, whereas black triggers perform better for attacks targeting the black class. The same trend persists under robust aggregation, showing that trigger color is a meaningful factor in the operation, persistence, and evaluation of semantic backdoor mechanisms in federated learning.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Beyond Corner Patches: Semantics-Aware Backdoor Attack in Federated Learning.
abstract: Backdoor attacks on federated learning (FL) are most often evaluated with synthetic corner patches or out-of-distribution (OOD) patterns that are unlikely to arise in practice. In this paper, we revisit the backdoor threat to standard FL (a single global model) under a more realistic setting where triggers must be semantically meaningful, in-distribution, and visually plausible. We propose SABLE, a Semantics-Aware Backdoor for LEarning in federated settings, which constructs natural, content-consistent triggers (e.g., semantic attribute changes such as sunglasses) and optimizes an aggregation-aware malicious objective with feature separation and parameter regularization to keep attacker updates close to benign ones. We instantiate SABLE on CelebA hair-color classification and the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB), poisoning only a small, interpretable subset of each malicious client’s local data while otherwise following the standard FL protocol. Across heterogeneous client partitions and multiple aggregation rules (FedAvg, Trimmed Mean, MultiKrum, FLAME and FilterFL), our semantics-driven triggers achieve high targeted attack success rates while preserving benign test accuracy. These results show that semantics-aligned backdoors remain a potent and practical threat in federated learning, and that robustness claims based solely on synthetic patch triggers can be overly optimistic.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: Preventing Human Errors for Dependable Computer System Design.
abstract: This tutorial provides participants with a systematic understanding of the fundamental theories underlying four key questions in designing and developing computer systems: why designers/developers commit errors, what kinds of errors they commit, when (under which conditions) they are most likely to commit errors, and how to use cognitive strategies to prevent errors. Building on these foundations, the tutorial presents faults and vulnerabilities from industrial projects to help participants identify underlying human-error causes. Participants will develop cognitive awareness of human errors across diverse project contexts, learn effective prevention strategies, and engage in interactive discussions to analyze trustworthiness issues from their own experiences. A curated list of human error prevention strategies will be provided for application in future projects. The training is essential for researchers, students, professional designers, and developers to design and develop trustworthy computer systems.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks

title: An Experimental Paradigm for Studying Cognitive Mechanisms Behind Software Faults.
abstract: This paper presents a new interdisciplinary experimental paradigm for studying the cognitive mechanisms behind software faults. We posit that programmers introduce the same faults because the development contexts contain scenarios that tend to trigger shared cognitive patterns-human error modes. To test the theory, we designed a new interdisciplinary experimental paradigm, in which a novel programming task was created with contexts associated with human error modes implicitly embedded, while not violating conventional requirements quality criteria, i.e., correctness, completeness, unambiguity, and consistency. We further conducted a controlled experiment involving 44 participants. The results show that human error modes are indeed a substantial cause of coincident faults. Further analysis reveals that coincident faults are not necessarily caused by difficulty; rather, they also occur at function locations that are easy but contain contexts that tend to trigger human error modes.
conference_title: International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks
